```{r}
library(fanogrid)
```

## The problem

Aggregating GPS points onto a grid fixes the spatial resolution of everything
computed downstream, so the grid size has to be chosen rather than assumed.
Selectors that minimise the mean integrated squared error do this by trading
sampling noise in a cell against variation of the density within it, and they
assume the points fall independently. GPS points do not: people travel with
family, friends and colleagues, which leaves groups of points a few metres
apart. A selector that assumes independence reads that lumpiness as structure in
the underlying density and asks for a finer grid than the data support.

The Fano factor measures how much of the variance in the cell counts exceeds the
Poisson level. Feeding it back into the cost function removes the part of the
variance that comes from people moving together.

## The data

`synthetic_gps` is one realisation of a clustered pattern whose underlying
density is piecewise constant on the 250-meter census grid, so the scale to
recover is known. `target_area` is the window it was generated over.

```{r}
str(synthetic_gps)
target_area
```

## What a Poisson selector chooses

`select_grid()` with `fano = 1` is the two-dimensional form of the
Shimazaki-Shinomoto selector.

```{r}
select_grid(synthetic_gps, target_area, fano = 1)
```

## Estimating the Fano factor

`estimate_fano()` needs a grid, because it holds the intensity constant within
each cell.

```{r}
estimate_fano(synthetic_gps, target_area, nx = 40, ny = 40)
```

## Estimating both together

`fanogrid()` alternates the two steps until the grid stops moving.

```{r}
fit <- fanogrid(synthetic_gps, target_area)
fit$delta
fit$fano
fit$trace
```

## Reading the result

The Poisson selector and `fanogrid()` are compared against the 250-meter scale
built into the data. This section is written once the estimators return numbers.
